description:
Is Erythritol Good or Bad for You? The Sweet Truth! 🍬

Erythritol—a natural sugar substitute that’s been making waves in the world of low-calorie sweeteners. But is it too good to be true? 🤔

In this video, we dive deep into the science of erythritol, exploring its health benefits, potential risks, and how it stacks up against other sweeteners in ice cream. Whether you’re curious about its effect on blood sugar, digestion, or how it fits into a healthy lifestyle, we’ve got you covered!

💡 Topics we cover:
 • What is erythritol, and how is it made?
 • Is erythritol safe for everyone?
 • Its impact on health.
 • It's use in ice cream and other foods.

Join me as I break down the facts and help you decide if erythritol is the right choice for you. Don’t forget to like, comment, and subscribe for more ice cream science.

#Erythritol #Sweeteners #FoodScience #HealthTips

comments.text: @PolarIceCreamery  so my perspective is, when using a creami, you can just re-process it before eating each time - its not really relevant to me whether or not it recrystalizes and is good right out of the freezer, since i can just re-spin it. my current method is to sweeten with a mix of a small amount of erythritol (i have some gut sensitivity to it), allulose (for most of the PAC, but im really only targeting a serving temp of like -8C), aspartame and acesulfame potassium (tiny amount to get the sweetness right), and some combination of inulin, cocoa powder, and protein powder to get the solids i need for decent texture. its not real ice cream in the sense that i cant just put it in the freezer and take it out and have it be scoopable after 5 minutes on the counter, but it blows basically every other light ice cream ive had out of the water.

comments.text:
I wonder then what could be substituted for sugars. My first attempt was just to see whether the machine worked well.    
But now I am trying to think about recipes. I have put the machine away for now since it's winter, but later on I wanted to experiment and get my own sweetspot for a protein ice cream.

Afaik the usual "milk flavoured" ice cream base that is used for soft serve ice creams usually have 10% butterfat content.   
So my first draft was: 
355 mL of whole milk
95 mL of cream (35%)
17 grams of erythritol

Which would result in 10% fat content. I had taken a usual ice cream base for milk flavour and divided the sugar by 3.   
Then I filled the other 2 components until it reached the desired number of 10% fat.   
I'd probably add 0.5 grams ice cream stabilizer as well to the mix.   

But apparently the fact that the sugars are a solid is also important to the ice cream. I had reckoned that would be the case but hoped it wouldn't be super important.    
I'm fine with the ice cream tasting less sweet (though I dunno how lackluster 17 grams of erythritol will be).     
I believe some soft serve recipes also use whey powder to give it a better texture. Which is great because whey isolate is also used as a protein supplement. Though I haven't researched that enough yet.
comments.author: @Titanicunillingus

comments.text: You’ve got no solids in there, the lack of sugars means there is way too much water when ch is freezing solid. Whey/Milk solids will help.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: I adapted the amazing Häagen-Dazs coffee ice cream to be sugar free. Unfortunately, it’s not low fat. I used 135 g of 2% fair life milk, 450 g of 33% heavy whipping cream, 175 g of espresso, 110 g of allulose , 65 g of insulin, 1/4 teaspoon of Guar gum, and liquid sucralose to increase the sweetness to taste. I believe I used between 15 to 20 drops. I followed the directions in the video to combine. I divided the mixture between two ninja creami pints, covered and chilled in the fridge for an hour before freezing. I only had to spin once after dishing some out I put the container back in the freezer. The next time. I do have to let it sit out a few minutes before scooping, but I don’t have to re-spin it.
